rules.filing: File the Article 989 Motion for Expungement with the proposed Article 991 Order and the proposed Article 992 Order of Expungement with the clerk of court in the parish of arrest or conviction. Article 972.1 gives district courts, city and parish courts, mayor's and traffic courts, juvenile and family courts, and the New Orleans municipal and traffic courts authority within their trial jurisdiction. Article 986 provides that only the forms in Articles 987, 988, 989, 990, 991, 992, 993, 994, 995 and 998 shall be used, so there is no drafted pleading and no local variant; Article 986(C) lets a clerk alter the form only to show the name of that court.
rules.notice: Under Article 980 any entity served under Article 979 may object by filing an affidavit of response, with reasons and with service on the defendant, within sixty days from the date of service of the motion. Since 1 August 2015 the Louisiana Bureau of Criminal Identification and Information is on the same sixty-day period as everyone else. Article 980(C) lets the court grant one extension of not more than thirty days beyond the original sixty. A timely objection means a contradictory hearing, which the objecting party must ask to have set. Where an Affidavit of No Opposition executed by each named agency is attached to the motion, the Article 991 Order states that no contradictory hearing is required and the motion may be granted ex parte. On the Article 978(E) lane a contradictory hearing is required by the Article itself, so the ex parte route is not available there and the objection window is not the operative constraint.
rules.service: The participant does not serve anyone. Under Article 979 the clerk of court serves notice of the motion by United States mail or electronically on the district attorney of the parish of conviction, the Louisiana Bureau of Criminal Identification and Information and the arresting law-enforcement agency, and files a certificate of service showing the mailing date. Under Article 982, if expungement is granted the clerk serves the order and judgment on the district attorney, the Bureau, the sheriff of the parish of conviction and the arresting agency.
rules.participantSignature: The mover signs the Article 989 Motion in the block headed 'If not represented by counsel'. LegalEase leaves the signature and date blank.
rules.fees: Article 983(A) caps the total cost at five hundred fifty dollars, collected by the clerk at filing and non-refundable even if the motion is denied. Where the conviction is for operating a vehicle while intoxicated, Article 984(C) assesses a further fifty-dollar court cost payable to the Office of Motor Vehicles. On the first offender pardon route the participant must also have paid the underlying court costs of the conviction, which is a precondition of the pardon rather than an expungement fee.
rules.feeWaiver: Article 983(F) through the Article 988 form in principle, but Louisiana State Police states that a person is ineligible for the exemption if they have ever been convicted of a felony, including an expunged felony. On a felony conviction track the exemption will almost never be available, and the packet says so rather than implying a waiver that will be refused.

generationRequirements.question: What is your full legal name as it appears on the arrest record — last, first, middle initial?
What is your date of birth?
What are the last four digits of your Social Security number?
What is your driver's license number?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked only where the participant holds or held a Louisiana driver's licence; the Article 989 form provides a field for it.

generationRequirements.question: Which judicial district or court handled the case?
In which parish were you arrested or convicted?
What is the docket or case number?
What division of the court is the case assigned to?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked where the participant's paperwork shows a division; the caption provides a field for it.

generationRequirements.question: Which law-enforcement agency arrested you?
On what date were you arrested? Use the arrest and booking date shown on your Louisiana State Police rap sheet, not the date of the offence.
What was each charge at the time of arrest? Give the original arrest charge and statute for every count, not the charge you were finally convicted of or the amended charge.
How many separate charges or counts are on this arrest?
What is your SID number, if your rap sheet shows one?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the Article 989 form provides the field; Louisiana State Police lists a missing or wrong identifier among its common fatal errors.

generationRequirements.question: What is the arrest number (ATN) shown on the rap sheet?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the Article 989 form provides the field and Louisiana State Police matches the motion to the rap sheet on it.

generationRequirements.question: What is the arresting agency's item number?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the Article 989 form provides the field.

generationRequirements.question: What felony offence were you convicted of, and under what statute?
On what date were you convicted?

Which applies to you — the conviction was set aside and the prosecution dismissed under Article 893(E); more than ten years have passed since you finished your sentence, probation or parole; you are entitled to a first offender pardon; or the offence is one of the six in Article 978(E)?
Has a court already signed an order setting aside the conviction and dismissing the prosecution under Article 893(E)?
Were you placed on probation under Article 893 with a deferred sentence, and did you complete the probation terms?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked where no Article 893(E) order exists, because it decides whether the participant should be routed to the Article 987 set-aside track first.

generationRequirements.question: On what date did you finish your sentence, deferred adjudication, probation or parole for this conviction?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked on the ten-year and Article 978(E) routes, because it starts the clean period.

generationRequirements.question: Since that date, have you been convicted of ANY other criminal offence — felony or misdemeanour, in any state?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked on the ten-year and Article 978(E) routes. Unlike the misdemeanour track, any criminal offence breaks this clean period, not only a felony.

generationRequirements.question: Is any criminal charge pending against you now?
Had you ever been convicted of a felony before this one?
Have all court costs for this conviction been paid?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked on the first offender pardon route. No pardon issues while court costs remain unpaid, and this is the common, fixable failure point.

generationRequirements.question: Is the offence a crime of violence under R.S. 14:2(B)?

Is the offence one of these six — aggravated battery, second degree battery, aggravated criminal damage to property, simple robbery, purse snatching, or illegal use of weapons or dangerous instrumentalities?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked where the offence is or may be a crime of violence, because Article 978(E) is the only lane that reaches those six.

generationRequirements.question: Is the offence a sex offence, or a criminal offence against a victim who is a minor, as defined by R.S. 15:541?
Is the offence a violation of the Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law?

If it is a drug offence, which of these fits — simple possession under R.S. 40:966(C), 967(C), 968(C), 969(C) or 970(C); possession with intent to distribute; an offence punishable by not more than five years; an offence eligible under Article 893(E); or an offence for which you are entitled to a first offender pardon?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked only where the offence is a controlled dangerous substance violation, because Article 978(B)(3) bars the class and then names five exceptions.

generationRequirements.question: Was the conviction for domestic abuse battery?
Was this conviction for operating a vehicle while intoxicated?
Does the record of this arrest name anyone besides you?
Are you now in the physical custody of the Department of Public Safety and Corrections serving a sentence at hard labour?

tracks.legalName: Interim Motion to Expunge a Felony Arrest from Criminal History (La. C.Cr.P. art. 985.1)
tracks.publicName: Clear a felony arrest that ended in a misdemeanor conviction
tracks.mechanism: Article 985.1(A) permits an interim motion to expunge a felony arrest from the criminal history of a person who was convicted of a misdemeanour offence arising out of that original felony arrest; only the original felony arrest is expunged. Article 985.1(B) makes the interim motion separate and distinct from expungement of a final conviction under Articles 976, 977 and 978. Article 985.1(C) applies the Article 979 et seq. procedures and fees except as provided in (D), and Article 985.1(D) provides that the motion is not subject to the time limitations of Article 977(A)(2) or 978(A)(2) and permits more than one interim expungement. Article 977(C)(1) expressly preserves interim expungement even where the misdemeanour conviction itself is barred by the sex-offence exclusion. Article 986 makes Article 994 the motion form and Article 995 the order form. Confirmed against the current official text; Article 985.1 has not been amended since Acts 2014, No. 145.
exclusions: The misdemeanour conviction itself is not expunged by this track. Only the original felony arrest entry is removed from the criminal history; the misdemeanour conviction remains on the record unless it is separately cleared under Article 977.
A person in the physical custody of the Department of Public Safety and Corrections serving a sentence at hard labour may not file (Art. 975).
There is no case-count limitation. Article 985.1(D) expressly permits more than one interim expungement.

waitingPeriods.condition: Interim expungement of the original felony arrest
waitingPeriods.duration: None. Article 985.1(D) expressly disapplies the Article 977(A)(2) five-year and Article 978(A)(2) ten-year time limitations.

rules.notice: Under Article 980 any entity served under Article 979 may object by filing an affidavit of response, with reasons and with service on the defendant, within sixty days from the date of service of the motion. Since 1 August 2015 the Louisiana Bureau of Criminal Identification and Information is on the same sixty-day period as everyone else. Article 980(C) lets the court grant one extension of not more than thirty days beyond the original sixty. A timely objection means a contradictory hearing, which the objecting party must ask to have set. Where an Affidavit of No Opposition executed by each named agency is attached to the motion, the Article 991 Order states that no contradictory hearing is required and the motion may be granted ex parte.
rules.service: The participant does not serve anyone. Under Article 979 the clerk of court serves notice of the motion by United States mail or electronically on the district attorney of the parish of conviction, the Louisiana Bureau of Criminal Identification and Information and the arresting law-enforcement agency, and files a certificate of service showing the mailing date. Under Article 982, if expungement is granted the clerk serves the order and judgment on the district attorney, the Bureau, the sheriff of the parish of conviction and the arresting agency.
rules.participantSignature: The mover signs the Article 994 Motion in the block for an unrepresented mover. LegalEase leaves the signature and date blank.
rules.fees: Article 985.1(C) applies the ordinary Article 983 fee provisions, so the five-hundred-fifty-dollar cap applies, collected by the clerk at filing and non-refundable even if the motion is denied.
rules.feeWaiver: Article 983(F) through the Article 988 Motion for Fee Exemption where its grounds are met.

tracks.legalName: Expungement by Redaction of Records with References to Multiple Individuals (La. C.Cr.P. art. 985)
tracks.publicName: Remove your name from a record you share with someone else
tracks.mechanism: Article 985(A) provides that if a record includes the name of more than one individual and one or more of them is entitled to an expungement of an arrest or conviction under Title XXXIV, any individual so entitled may petition the court to have records related to that individual's arrest or conviction expunged by redaction. Article 985(B) provides that if the court grants expungement by redaction, the name of the individual and all other identifying information regarding that individual shall be redacted from all records regarding the arrest and conviction, and the redacted records remain available for public access. Article 985(C) relieves the clerk of liability where the order does not specifically identify all locations of the records to be expunged or specify the information to be redacted. Article 972(3) defines the term. The relief runs on the Article 989 motion and the Article 992 order, whose text contains the dedicated redaction paragraph. Confirmed against the current official text; Article 985 has not been amended since Acts 2014, No. 145.
exclusions: A person who is not independently entitled to an expungement of the arrest or conviction under Title XXXIV. Article 985 is a form of relief for someone already entitled under Article 976, 977 or 978; it is not an independent eligibility ground.
A record that names only the petitioner. Where no other individual appears in the record there is nothing to redact and the ordinary expungement track applies instead.
A person in the physical custody of the Department of Public Safety and Corrections serving a sentence at hard labour may not file (Art. 975).

Under Article 982, if expungement is granted the clerk serves the order and judgment on the district attorney, the Bureau, the sheriff of the parish of conviction and the arresting agency.
rules.participantSignature: The mover signs the Article 989 Motion in the block headed 'If not represented by counsel'. LegalEase leaves the signature and date blank.
rules.fees: Article 983(A) caps the total cost at five hundred fifty dollars, collected by the clerk at filing and non-refundable even if the motion is denied.
rules.feeWaiver: Article 983(F) through the Article 988 Motion for Fee Exemption where the underlying basis meets its grounds.

tracks.legalName: Expedited Expungement of Arrest Records for Certain Individuals (La. C.Cr.P. arts. 999, 999.1)
tracks.publicName: Free expedited clearing of an arrest from when you were seventeen
tracks.mechanism: Article 999(A) provides that a person shall be entitled to the expedited expungement of his arrest, at no cost to him, if the person meets all of the following: (1) the person is seventeen years of age when arrested or charged with any criminal offence under Title 14 or Title 40 of the Louisiana Revised Statutes of 1950; (2) the district attorney, for any reason, declined to prosecute all offences arising out of that arrest, including because the person successfully completed a pretrial diversion programme; and (3) prosecution was instituted and such proceedings have been finally disposed of by dismissal, sustaining of a motion to quash, or acquittal. Article 999(B) provides that the Article does not apply to any misdemeanour or felony conviction arising from the incident of arrest. Article 999(C) provides that the expedited expungement shall be served under Article 982. Article 972(1) defines expedited expungement as an order of expungement that a judge may sign pursuant to Article 999 WITHOUT THE INDIVIDUAL FILING A MOTION TO EXPUNGE WITH THE CLERK OF COURT. Article 999.1 supplies the order form to be used, which recites the three Article 999(A) conditions, provides the defendant-information fields and a six-entry service list, and carries the judge's signature line. Both Articles were added, and Articles 972 and 983(G) amended, by Acts 2024, No. 270, effective 1 August 2024.
exclusions: Any misdemeanour or felony conviction arising from the incident of arrest (Art. 999(B)).

A person who was not seventeen years of age when arrested or charged. The age element is objective and narrow: it is a legacy of Louisiana's raise-the-age transition and is not a general youthful-offender provision.
An arrest or charge for an offence outside Title 14 or Title 40 of the Louisiana Revised Statutes of 1950.

Applied as written, Article 999(A) requires all three conditions together, which means the route reaches only a person who was seventeen at arrest AND whose offences the district attorney declined to prosecute AND whose instituted prosecution was finally disposed of by dismissal, quashal or acquittal. This memo applies the statute as written because that is the narrower reading; the internal contradiction between (2) and (3) is preserved as an open question rather than resolved by construction.

releaseBlockers.question: Article 999(A) says the person must meet 'all of the following' and then lists (2) a declination to prosecute all offences arising out of the arrest and (3) an instituted prosecution finally disposed of by dismissal, quashal or acquittal. Read literally the two are mutually exclusive, because a declination means no prosecution was instituted, and almost nobody could qualify. The Acts 2024, No. 270 résumé digest repeats 'all of the following', and the Article 999.1 order form recites the same three conditions under the heading 'wherein all of the following applies', so both the statute and the prescribed order carry the cumulative formulation. Whether (2) and (3) are cumulative as written or alternative as they must sensibly be is unresolved, and it materially decides who the eligibility engine returns.

tracks.legalName: Automated Expungement of Qualifying Records (La. C.Cr.P. art. 985.2)
tracks.publicName: Louisiana's automated expungement process
tracks.mechanism: Article 985.2(A) directs the Louisiana Bureau of Criminal Identification and Information to identify within its criminal repository database all records with a Case Management Information System number and final dispositions for individuals eligible for expungement under Articles 976, 977 and 978. Article 985.2(B) provides that beginning 1 January 2025 a defendant may submit a request through the Bureau for expungement through the automated process, the request containing the defendant's name, date of birth, last four digits of the Social Security number, arrest date and case number, and requires the Bureau to expunge any eligible records within thirty days of receipt and send them to the Louisiana Supreme Court Case Management Information System. Paragraphs (C) and (D) govern clerk verification and notice to the district attorney, sheriff and arresting agency. Article 985.2(G) provides that the Article shall be subject to the appropriate funding necessary for implementation and provided for in the executive budget for Fiscal Year 2025-2026. The current official text at legis.la.gov carries the operative note 'Article 985.2 eff. upon appropriation of monies by the Legislature. See Acts 2023, No. 454.' Section 4 of Acts 2023, No. 454 conditions the effectiveness of its substantive Sections on an Act or Acts originating in the 2023 Regular Session containing specific appropriations of monies for the office of state police, the Louisiana Supreme Court and the Louisiana Clerks' Remote Access Authority for the implementation of the Act. The route reaches only records already eligible under Articles 976, 977 and 978 and expands eligibility for no one.
exclusions: The Article is not established as effective. The current official text of the Code carries the note that Article 985.2 is effective upon appropriation of monies by the Legislature, citing Acts 2023, No. 454, and that note is still present on the Legislature's own current publication of the Article as of 3 August 2026.

The route does not expand eligibility. It reaches only records already eligible for expungement under Articles 976, 977 and 978, so a person not already eligible under those Articles gains nothing from it.
Records predating the automation window described in the Article are outside it.
The enacting legislation provided that no person shall have a cause of action resulting from the omission of their records from automated expungement.

tracks.legalName: Immediate Expungement; Judicial Discretion (La. C.Cr.P. art. 985.3)
tracks.publicName: Immediate clearing by the court after you finish probation or a program
tracks.mechanism: Article 985.3(A) provides that the court MAY ORDER the immediate expungement of the record of the arrest and conviction of the violation that necessitated participation in the probation or programme, by a person who is otherwise eligible for an expungement, upon the successful completion of a court-ordered probation or alternative sentencing programme. Article 985.3(B) provides that ONLY THE FORM PROVIDED IN ARTICLE 992 shall be used to expunge the record of such a person. Article 985.3(C) provides that the immediate expungement shall be served pursuant to Article 982 and shall include the court record with the signed order together with the bill of information, the sentencing minutes, and any documents or records relevant to the arrest incident and plea agreements, if available. releaseBlockers.question: Whether a defendant may move for Article 985.3 relief, and if so by what vehicle. Article 985.3(A) says the court 'may order' the immediate expungement and prescribes no motion, application or request; Article 985.3(B) names only the Article 992 order form; Article 986's mandatory-form list assigns no motion form to the Article; and the Acts 2024, No. 560 digest describes it as a court-ordered automatic expungement. Whether in practice the court acts on its own at the completion or discharge proceeding, or whether the defendant presents an ordinary Article 989 motion and asks the court to exercise Article 985.3 discretion, is not answered by any official source. If the latter, the participant-facing packet is the Article 989 and 992 pair already modelled on the Article 977 and 978 tracks, and this track would become a routing node into them rather than an independent packet.

releaseBlockers.question: Whether Article 985.3 displaces the Article 977(A)(2) five-year and Article 978(A)(2) ten-year waiting periods for a person who is otherwise eligible and has successfully completed a court-ordered probation or alternative sentencing programme. tracks.legalName: Motion to Set Aside Conviction and Dismiss Prosecution; Rule to Show Cause; Order of Dismissal (La. C.Cr.P. art. 987)
tracks.publicName: Set aside a conviction and dismiss the prosecution after a deferred sentence
tracks.mechanism: Article 987 supplies the forms to be used for a motion to set aside a conviction and dismiss the prosecution, the rule to show cause, and the order of dismissal. It is not an expungement. It is the predicate filing that converts a completed deferred sentence into a set-aside conviction and a dismissed prosecution under Article 894(B) for a misdemeanour or Article 893(E) for a felony, which in turn unlocks Article 977(A)(1) or Article 978(A)(1). As pleaded on the statutory form, eligibility is that the period of the deferred sentence has run and the petitioner has successfully completed the terms of probation. The instrument is in three parts: the Motion; a Rule to Show Cause ordering the district attorney to show cause why the motion should not be granted; and the Order of Dismissal. The motion's own prayer asks for relief after a contradictory hearing with the district attorney's office. Service is on the district attorney and on the attorney for the defendant or the defendant. The form carries parallel signature blocks for counsel and for an unrepresented mover, so it is drafted for pro se use. Source note Acts 2014, No. 145.
exclusions: A conviction that was not the subject of a deferred sentence under Article 893 or Article 894. Where no deferred sentence was imposed there is nothing to set aside, and the participant goes directly to the Article 977 or Article 978 waiting-period route instead.
A case where the period of the deferred sentence has not yet run.

rules.filing: File the three-part Article 987 instrument — Motion, Rule to Show Cause and Order of Dismissal — with the clerk of the court that imposed the deferred sentence, in the parish of conviction. Article 986 makes Article 987 the form to be used, so there is nothing to draft; Article 986(C) lets a clerk alter it only to show the name of that court.
rules.fees: Article 983 governs the cost of an expungement, not of an Article 987 set-aside. Ordinary court costs for filing a motion may apply and vary by parish; the packet tells the participant to ask the clerk of the sentencing court what the filing cost is rather than stating a figure the Code does not fix.
rules.feeWaiver: none prescribed by Article 987. The Article 988 fee exemption is an expungement instrument under Article 983(F) and does not reach this filing.
rules.notice: The Rule to Show Cause orders the district attorney to show cause why the motion should not be granted, and the motion's prayer asks for relief after a contradictory hearing with the district attorney's office. No sixty-day objection window applies; that scheme belongs to Articles 979 and 980 and governs a motion to expunge.
rules.service: Service is on the district attorney and on the attorney for the defendant or the defendant.
rules.participantSignature: The mover signs the Article 987 Motion in the block for an unrepresented mover. LegalEase leaves the signature and date blank.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Seal under G.L. c. 276, § 100A
tracks.publicName: Sealing your record through Probation
tracks.mechanism: On a form furnished by the Commissioner of Probation and signed under the penalties of perjury, the Commissioner shall seal a record once the statutory period has run. Relief is mandatory and ministerial: no judge is involved, the Commissioner has no discretion to refuse, and no reasons are given. The 2018 Criminal Justice Reform Act cut the waits from five and ten years to three and seven.
exclusions: Convictions under G.L. c. 140, §§ 121 to 131H (firearms), except as part of a delinquency record.
Convictions under G.L. c. 268 or c. 268A, except resisting arrest, which may be sealed.
A person who has at any time been classified as a level 2 or level 3 sex offender under G.L. c. 6, § 178K may not seal sex offences at all.

A guilty finding in Massachusetts within the applicable lookback, or a conviction or imprisonment in another state, a United States possession or a federal court in that window, excepting motor vehicle offences punishable by a fine of not more than $50.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge under G.L. c. 276, §§ 100F, 100G and 100H
tracks.publicName: Expunging a record from before you turned 21
tracks.mechanism: Time-based expungement requires all offences to have occurred before the person's 21st birthday, a record of not more than two convictions or two non-conviction records, and three years for a misdemeanour-only record or seven where any felony is involved. The architecture is genuinely staged: the Commissioner of Probation certifies eligibility under §§ 100I and 100J, and only then does the matter reach a judge with the district attorney on notice.
exclusions: The § 100J list: offences resulting in death or serious bodily injury; offences committed with intent to cause death or serious bodily injury; offences involving a dangerous weapon; offences against an elderly or disabled person; sex offences, child sex offences and sexually violent offences; operating under the influence under c. 90 § 24; firearms offences under c. 140 §§ 121 to 131Q; violations of abuse prevention and harassment prevention orders; and domestic assault and battery under c. 265 § 13M.
Any offence occurring on or after the person's 21st birthday. All offences must have occurred before it.
More than two records. Multiple offences arising from the same incident count as one.

Any other Massachusetts criminal or juvenile appearance or disposition, and any out-of-state, United States possession or federal appearance or disposition, excepting minor motor vehicle offences and the records being expunged.
Being the subject of an active criminal investigation.

tracks.mechanism: Section 100K reaches a record created by false identification or identity theft, an offence that is no longer a crime, demonstrable errors by law enforcement, by civilian or expert witnesses, or by court employees, or demonstrable fraud on the court. The court must find on clear and convincing evidence that the record was created on one of the grounds, then exercises discretion on the best interests of justice.
exclusions: None. Section 100K operates notwithstanding §§ 100I and 100J, so the under-21 rule, the two-record cap and the § 100J exclusion list do not apply. This is the most important structural fact about the track and the internal reference does not state it.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Records under Md. Code, Criminal Procedure § 10-105
tracks.publicName: Expungement of a case that did not end in a conviction
tracks.mechanism: Police, court and other State or local records may be expunged on petition for the § 10-105(a) favorable dispositions. Absent a timely State's Attorney objection § 10-105(d)(2) directs the court to pass the order; Maryland appellate law holds a court has no discretion to deny where statutory entitlement is shown. As amended by the Expungement Reform Act of 2025, effective October 1, 2025.
exclusions: A PBJ entered on a charge under Transportation § 21-902(c), (d), (h) or (i), Criminal Law Title 2 Subtitle 5, or Criminal Law § 3-211, is not eligible at all under § 10-105(a)(3).

The § 10-105(a-1) carve-out for a pre-October 1, 2020 sodomy conviction or a pre-October 1, 2023 § 3-322 violation committed without consent, with a minor under 16, with a person the individual could not marry under Family Law § 2-202, or with a mentally incapacitated, physically helpless or substantially cognitively impaired individual.
Non-incarcerable vehicle-law and traffic violations, per the form's own affirmation.
The unit rule under § 10-107(b)(1), subject to the minor-traffic and cannabis-possession carve-outs in § 10-107(a).
Ineligible while a defendant in a pending criminal proceeding, § 10-105(e)(4)(iii).

For a PBJ, a conviction within 3 years of the PBJ other than a minor traffic violation or an act no longer a crime, § 10-105(e)(4)(i); extended to 15 years for a § 21-902(a) or (b) PBJ under § 10-105(e)(4)(ii).

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of a Conviction under Md. Code, Criminal Procedure § 10-110
tracks.publicName: Expungement of an eligible conviction
tracks.mechanism: Convictions on the § 10-110(a) enumerated list may be expunged after the applicable period from completion of the sentence. Absent objection § 10-110(e)(3) makes the order mandatory. On a timely objection by the State's Attorney or a victim, § 10-110(f)(2) requires a hearing and five findings on the record. SB 432 (2025) overrode In re Expungement Petition of Abhishek I., so a probation violation no longer automatically disqualifies.
exclusions: Any conviction not on the § 10-110(a) enumerated list. Violent offenses, most serious felonies and registrable sex offenses are outside the list.
DUI and DWI convictions are not on the list; only a PBJ or other non-conviction outcome reaches the § 10-105 route.
Conviction of a new crime during the applicable waiting period, unless that new conviction is itself eligible for expungement, § 10-110(d).
Defendant in a pending criminal proceeding.
Unit rule under § 10-107, subject to the (a) carve-outs.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement After a Full and Unconditional Pardon
tracks.publicName: Expungement after a pardon from the Governor
tracks.mechanism: Where the person is convicted of only one criminal act, that act is not a crime of violence as defined in Criminal Law § 14-101(a), and the Governor grants a full and unconditional pardon, the record may be expunged. The petition may not be filed later than 10 years after the Governor signed the pardon.
exclusions: Crimes of violence as defined in Criminal Law § 14-101(a).
Persons convicted of more than one criminal act.
Petitions filed more than 10 years after the Governor signed the pardon.

waitingPeriods.condition: The Governor signs a full and unconditional pardon
waitingPeriods.duration: None, but the petition may not be filed later than 10 years after the pardon signature. This is a deadline, not a waiting period.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Shielding Under the Maryland Second Chance Act
tracks.publicName: Shielding a conviction from public view
tracks.mechanism: Twelve enumerated convictions may be shielded from public view three years after the sentence for all convictions for which shielding is requested is satisfied, including parole, probation or mandatory supervision. One shielding petition will be granted per lifetime, in one court in one county, and must include every eligible conviction from that court. Under § 10-305 a shielded conviction is not a conviction for the subsequent-conviction rule.
exclusions: Any conviction outside the twelve enumerated offences.
Domestically related convictions.
A pending criminal matter.
The unit rule.
A new conviction during the three-year window, unless that conviction is itself shieldable.
A second shielding petition. One will be granted, ever.

waitingPeriods.condition: Satisfaction of the sentence for all convictions for which shielding is requested, including parole, probation or mandatory supervision

tracks.legalName: Automatic Expungement of Qualifying Non-Conviction Cases under § 10-105.1
tracks.publicName: Automatic clearing of a case that ended without a conviction
tracks.mechanism: For a civil offence under Criminal Law § 5-601(c)(2)(ii) or a crime other than a Transportation Article violation for which the defendant is not required to appear, where no charge in the case resulted in a disposition other than acquittal, dismissal, not guilty or nolle prosequi excluding nolle with a treatment requirement, the record shall be expunged three years after disposition, beginning October 1, 2021. No petition, no fee, no filing. The court notifies the Central Repository, custodians and the person, and under § 10-105.2 must notify the defendant of the right at disposition with a General Waiver and Release form.
exclusions: Cases where any charge resulted in a disposition other than the four qualifying outcomes.
Nolle prosequi entered with a drug or alcohol treatment requirement.
Transportation Article violations for which the defendant is required to appear.

waitingPeriods.condition: Disposition, for cases disposed on or after October 1, 2021
waitingPeriods.duration: 3 years, automatic

tracks.venue: No venue. There is no participant filing on this track.

destination.name: The court and the Central Repository
destination.detail: The court sends notice of the disposition and the required expungement date to the Central Repository, each booking facility, law enforcement unit and other State or local unit that may hold a record, and to the person entitled to expungement. Nothing is filed by the participant.

On written denial, or on failure to act within 60 days, the person may apply to the District Court with proper venue within 30 days of the denial, on DC-CR-071, which prints Rules Forms 4-503.3 and 4-503.4. The agency has 30 days after service to answer with specific grounds.
exclusions: Incidents occurring on or after October 1, 2007, which use the automatic police-record route.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Seal Criminal History Record Information (15 M.R.S. ch. 310-A, §§ 2262-2264)
tracks.publicName: Sealing a Maine criminal conviction
tracks.mechanism: Chapter 310-A permits a person to move, in the underlying criminal proceeding, to seal the criminal history record information relating to one specific eligible criminal conviction. Under § 2262 the conviction must be an eligible criminal conviction; at least four years must have passed since the person fully satisfied each of the sentencing alternatives imposed under 17-A M.R.S. § 1502(2); the person must not have been convicted of another crime in Maine and must not have had a criminal charge dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition since satisfying the sentence for their most recent eligible criminal conviction; must not have been convicted of a crime in another jurisdiction in that period; and must have no presently pending criminal charges in Maine or elsewhere. Former § 2262(6), an age condition, was repealed by PL 2023, c. 666, § 3. 'Eligible criminal conviction' under § 2261(6)(A) means a current or former Class E crime other than one under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 11, and under § 2261(6)(B) five specifically listed marijuana offences committed before 30 January 2017. Relief is mandatory once proven: § 2264(5) directs that the court shall grant the motion where the person establishes each prerequisite by a preponderance of the evidence. A hearing is required and the Maine Rules of Evidence do not apply (§ 2264(4)). The current text reflects PL 2021, c. 674 as amended by PL 2023, cc. 409, 639 and 666 and PL 2025, c. 513, which became law without the Governor’s signature on 11 January 2026 and took effect on 29 July 2026.
exclusions: Every Class A, Class B and Class C crime. Chapter 310-A does not reach them.
Every Class D crime other than the five listed marijuana offences committed before 30 January 2017.
A current or former Class E crime under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 11 (sexual assaults), excluded by § 2261(6)(A).

A conviction of another crime in Maine, a criminal charge dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition under 17-A M.R.S. former ch. 54-F or ch. 67 subch. 4, or a conviction in another jurisdiction, in each case since the person fully satisfied the sentence for their most recent eligible criminal conviction (§ 2262(3) and (4)).
Any presently pending criminal charge in Maine or in another jurisdiction (§ 2262(5)).

A non-conviction disposition. § 2262 reaches a specific criminal conviction only, and filing this motion on a non-conviction is affirmatively wrong; those records are handled by operation of law under 16 M.R.S. § 703(2).
The exclusion set is the defining fact about Maine: the ordinary adult route reaches almost nothing, and the product's most valuable function here is to say no accurately and quickly.

waitingPeriods.condition: Every eligible criminal conviction
waitingPeriods.duration: Four years from the date the person fully satisfied EACH of the sentencing alternatives imposed under 17-A M.R.S. § 1502(2) — imprisonment, probation, administrative release, licence suspension, fine payments, restitution and community service. The clock does not start at conviction and does not start at release, and an unpaid restitution or fine balance means it has not started at all.

generationRequirements.question: What is your full legal name as it appears on the court record, and any other name you were charged under?
What is your date of birth?
Which court entered the conviction — Superior Court, District Court, or the Unified Criminal Docket?
Which county and court location was that?
What is the docket number of the criminal case?
What crime were you convicted of, as it is named on the judgment?
On what date were you convicted?
What class of crime was it at the time you were convicted — Class E, Class D, or something else? Use the class shown on the judgment, not the class the offence carries today.
Was the offence a sexual assault offence under Title 17-A, chapter 11?
Was this a marijuana offence committed before 30 January 2017?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked where the offence is a Class D crime, because the only Class D route is the five listed pre-2017 marijuana offences.

generationRequirements.question: What did your sentence include — jail or prison, probation, administrative release, licence suspension, a fine, restitution, community service, or a combination?
On what date did you finish the LAST of those, including paying every fine and every dollar of restitution in full? If any balance is still owed, say so.
Since that date, have you been convicted of any other crime in Maine?

Since that date, has any criminal charge against you been dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition? People often describe this as 'it got dismissed', and it is a disqualifier here, so please answer carefully.
Since that date, have you been convicted of a crime in any other state, in a federal court, or in a tribal court?
Do you have any criminal charge pending right now, in Maine or anywhere else?
Do you have any Maine adult criminal conviction that is OLDER than the date you finished the sentence for this conviction?
Have you already asked a court to seal this conviction and been denied?

manualCompletionItems.item: Paragraph 3 of CR-218 — the assertion of no other adult criminal convictions in Maine
manualCompletionItems.why: Paragraph 3 of CR-218 Rev. 7/24 reads in full: 'Defendant has no other adult criminal convictions in Maine and has not had a case dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition since completing their sentence for this offense.' The trailing time limit governs the deferred-disposition clause but not the convictions clause, so the form asks the participant to swear to an unbounded absence of Maine convictions while § 2262(3) bars only a conviction SINCE the person fully satisfied the sentence for their most recent eligible criminal conviction. A participant with an old prior that predates the completion date is not disqualified by the statute but reads as disqualified on the form. LegalEase does not answer this paragraph either way: it prints it blank, sets out both readings in plain terms, and tells the participant to complete it themselves and to take advice before filing if they have an older prior.

manualCompletionItems.item: Paragraph 1's assertion that the crime is eligible for sealing under 15 M.R.S. § 2261(6)
manualCompletionItems.why: Whether a crime is a current or former Class E crime, and whether a pre-2017 marijuana offence matches one of the five listed subparagraphs, is a legal conclusion requiring the judgment and the historical statute. The participant owns it.

releaseBlockers.question: Whether a chapter 310-A sealing order removes the case from Maine's public court record search. 15 M.R.S. § 2265 makes the conviction confidential criminal history record information and restricts dissemination by a criminal justice agency, and § 2264(6) makes the State Bureau of Identification amend its records. But 16 M.R.S. § 708(3)(A) provides that the Criminal History Record Information Act does not apply to criminal history record information contained in the records of public judicial proceedings retained by the District Court, Superior Court or Supreme Judicial Court, and that public access to those records is as provided by rule or administrative order of the Supreme Judicial Court. § 2265 opens 'Notwithstanding Title 16, section 704' and does not mention section 708. Participant-facing copy must therefore say that sealing restricts what criminal justice agencies may disseminate and what appears on a State Bureau of Identification check, and must not say or imply that the court case disappears from a public docket search.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Seal Criminal Conviction for Engaging in Prostitution (15 M.R.S. § 2262-A)
tracks.publicName: Sealing a conviction for engaging in prostitution
tracks.mechanism: Section 2262-A permits sealing of criminal history record information relating to a conviction for the former Class E crime of engaging in prostitution under 17-A M.R.S. former § 853-A, repealed in 2023. The person must not have been convicted of a violation of 17-A M.R.S. §§ 852, 853, 853-B or 855, or of substantially similar conduct in another jurisdiction, and one year must have passed since the person fully satisfied each sentencing alternative for the conviction. Section 2262 opens 'Except as provided in sections 2262-A and 2262-B', so the general track's clean-record conditions in § 2262(3) and (4) and its pending-charge restriction in § 2262(5) do NOT apply here. Relief is mandatory: the information must be sealed if the conditions are met, and § 2264(5) requires the court to grant on a preponderance showing. releaseBlockers.question: Whether a chapter 310-A sealing order removes the case from Maine's public court record search. 15 M.R.S. § 2265 makes the conviction confidential criminal history record information and restricts dissemination by a criminal justice agency, and § 2264(6) makes the State Bureau of Identification amend its records. But 16 M.R.S. § 708(3)(A) provides that the Criminal History Record Information Act does not apply to criminal history record information contained in the records of public judicial proceedings retained by the District Court, Superior Court or Supreme Judicial Court, and that public access to those records is as provided by rule or administrative order of the Supreme Judicial Court. § 2265 opens 'Notwithstanding Title 16, section 704' and does not mention section 708. Participant-facing copy must therefore say that sealing restricts what criminal justice agencies may disseminate and what appears on a State Bureau of Identification check, and must not say or imply that the court case disappears from a public docket search.

tracks.legalName: Confidential Criminal History Record Information for Non-Conviction Dispositions, and the § 709 Inspection and Correction Request (16 M.R.S. ch. 7)
tracks.publicName: Cases that did not end in a conviction
tracks.mechanism: Maine does not seal or expunge non-convictions on motion. Under 16 M.R.S. § 703(2) the listed non-conviction dispositions are confidential criminal history record information BY OPERATION OF LAW, with no filing and no court involvement: a summons or arrest without disposition where more than one year has elapsed, no active prosecution is pending and the person is not a fugitive; a decision by law enforcement not to refer to a prosecutor; a decision by a prosecutor not to initiate or approve criminal proceedings; a grand jury finding of insufficient evidence; a charge dismissed with prejudice by the court or dismissed with finality by a prosecutor outside a plea agreement; an acquittal, which does not include a verdict or accepted plea of not criminally responsible by reason of insanity; a mistrial with prejudice; termination for lack of subject matter jurisdiction; termination for want of jurisdiction over the defendant; and the remaining paragraphs of § 703(2), which include a pardoned conviction. Confidential information may be disseminated only to the recipients listed in § 705, and a criminal justice agency may not confirm its existence or nonexistence to anyone not entitled to receive it. Separately, § 709 gives a person the right to inspect their own criminal history record information held by a Maine criminal justice agency and to request that it be amended or corrected: the agency has fifteen days to investigate and notify the requester with reasons for any refusal, the agency head must complete an administrative appeal within thirty days, a person denied on appeal may file a statement of disagreement that must accompany any future dissemination, final agency action is appealable to the Superior Court under 5 M.R.S. ch. 375 subch. 7, and on correction the agency must notify prior recipients within thirty days. Section 709(6) provides that the section does not apply to court records, access to which is governed by Supreme Judicial Court rules.

units.label: Confidentiality by operation of law — classification and verification, no filing
units.description: The base branch. Where the disposition falls inside the 16 M.R.S. § 703(2) list the record is already confidential criminal history record information and there is nothing to file: no court has any role, no motion exists, and generating CR-218 for a non-conviction would be affirmatively wrong because § 2262 reaches a specific criminal conviction only. The unit classifies the disposition against the § 703(2) list, explains that the confidentiality is automatic, walks the participant through obtaining their own State Bureau of Identification record to see what the State actually holds, and states plainly where the disposition falls outside the list that Maine offers no relief for it rather than routing them to a motion that will be denied. It also separates the three problems that participants conflate: the Bureau record, the court docket, and a private vendor's database.

units.label: 16 M.R.S. § 709 inspection and correction request to the criminal justice agency
units.description: The conditional branch, reached only where the agency record is demonstrably inaccurate — most often where the State Bureau of Identification is still carrying a disposition that § 703(2) makes confidential, or is carrying a disposition that is simply wrong. § 709(1) and (2) give the participant the right to inspect their own criminal history record information and to request that it be amended or corrected by contacting the agency, and the agency then has fifteen days to investigate and notify the requester with reasons for any refusal. No official Maine form exists for the request and none is prescribed by the statute, so this is a participant-signed written request that LegalEase drafts: it identifies the participant and the record, states the disposition and its § 703(2) category, states precisely what the agency record says and what it should say, attaches the disposition order, and asks for amendment or correction under § 709(2). The packet also carries the escalation path — administrative appeal to the agency head within thirty days, the statement of disagreement that must accompany any future dissemination, and Superior Court review of final agency action under 5 M.R.S. ch. 375 subch. 7 — as instructions rather than as generated documents. This unit is a separate legal act from unit 1: it has a participant submission, a named destination, its own statutory basis and its own legal output, where unit 1 has none of those.

releaseBlockers.question: Whether a charge dismissed after successful completion of a deferred disposition under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 67 subch. 4 is confidential criminal history record information under 16 M.R.S. § 703(2). This was checked against current official text and is NOT ESTABLISHED. Section 703(2) lists paragraphs A through L and none mentions a deferred disposition. The closest is paragraph G, which reaches a charge 'dismissed with prejudice by the court or dismissed with finality by a prosecutor outside a plea agreement'. Under 17-A M.R.S. § 1903 the State dismisses the charging instrument WITH PREJUDICE on compliance, which fits the first clause, but a deferred disposition arises from a written agreement between the defendant and the State, which arguably falls inside paragraph G's outside-a-plea-agreement carve-out. Section 1903 says nothing about confidentiality or sealing. No statute, State Bureau of Identification guidance, Judicial Branch page or Law Court decision resolves it. The packet therefore fails closed: it does not promise confidentiality on the strength of the deferred-disposition label, it tells the participant to verify what the Bureau record actually shows, and it routes the correction request only where the record is demonstrably inaccurate.

provenance.sourceStatement: Whether a charge dismissed after successful completion of a deferred disposition is confidential under § 703(2). § 703(5) lists "a deferred disposition" as a disposition type, and the dismissal that follows is typically a dismissal, but whether it is a dismissal "with prejudice" or "with finality by a prosecutor other than as part of a plea agreement" is not settled on the face of the statute. A deferred disposition in Maine follows a guilty plea, which makes the plea-agreement carve-out a live question. Build blocker for routing deferred-disposition participants.
provenance.counselQuestion: Does a 17-A M.R.S. § 1903 dismissal after a completed deferred disposition fall inside 16 M.R.S. § 703(2)(G), given that it is a dismissal with prejudice but arises from a written agreement with the State? Until answered, LegalEase promises no confidentiality on this branch.

The packet says so plainly rather than implying the docket is cured.

tracks.legalName: Deferred Disposition — Outcome Classification and Sealing-Eligibility Routing (17-A M.R.S. ch. 67, subch. 4; 15 M.R.S. § 2262(3))
tracks.publicName: Cases resolved through a deferred disposition
tracks.mechanism: A deferred disposition is not a record-clearing mechanism and produces no relief of its own. It is a disposition status with two possible outcomes and one sharp cross-track consequence, and it is modelled as a routing node for exactly that reason. Under 17-A M.R.S. § 1901 a deferred disposition arises from a written agreement between the defendant and the State; under § 1903, on compliance and the State's motion, the court permits withdrawal of the plea and the State dismisses the charging instrument with prejudice. Section 1903 says nothing about confidentiality or sealing. Where the case instead ends in conviction of a reduced offence, that conviction is evaluated on its own terms under chapter 310-A and qualifies only if it lands inside the § 2261(6) eligible set. The cross-track consequence is the one that matters most: under 15 M.R.S. § 2262(3) a criminal charge dismissed as the result of a deferred disposition, since the person fully satisfied the sentence for their most recent eligible criminal conviction, is an absolute disqualifier for the general sealing track. A deferred disposition is therefore good news for the case it resolves and bad news for a prior conviction the participant wanted sealed.
exclusions: This node produces no relief and no packet of its own. It is not a sealing remedy, it is not a paid-packet route, and no deferred-disposition sealing packet is generated.
A deferred disposition still in its deferral period. Nothing is routed until the outcome is known.

releaseBlockers.question: Whether a charge dismissed after successful completion of a deferred disposition under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 67 subch. 4 is confidential criminal history record information under 16 M.R.S. § 703(2). This was checked against current official text and is NOT ESTABLISHED. Section 703(2) lists paragraphs A through L and none mentions a deferred disposition. The closest is paragraph G, which reaches a charge 'dismissed with prejudice by the court or dismissed with finality by a prosecutor outside a plea agreement'. Under 17-A M.R.S. § 1903 the State dismisses the charging instrument WITH PREJUDICE on compliance, which fits the first clause, but a deferred disposition arises from a written agreement between the defendant and the State, which arguably falls inside paragraph G's outside-a-plea-agreement carve-out. Section 1903 says nothing about confidentiality or sealing. No statute, State Bureau of Identification guidance, Judicial Branch page or Law Court decision resolves it. The packet therefore fails closed: it does not promise confidentiality on the strength of the deferred-disposition label, it tells the participant to verify what the Bureau record actually shows, and it routes the correction request only where the record is demonstrably inaccurate.

provenance.sourceStatement: Whether a charge dismissed after successful completion of a deferred disposition is confidential under § 703(2). § 703(5) lists "a deferred disposition" as a disposition type, and the dismissal that follows is typically a dismissal, but whether it is a dismissal "with prejudice" or "with finality by a prosecutor other than as part of a plea agreement" is not settled on the face of the statute. A deferred disposition in Maine follows a guilty plea, which makes the plea-agreement carve-out a live question. Build blocker for routing deferred-disposition participants.
provenance.counselQuestion: Does a 17-A M.R.S. § 1903 dismissal after a completed deferred disposition fall inside 16 M.R.S. § 703(2)(G), given that it is a dismissal with prejudice but arises from a written agreement with the State? Until answered, LegalEase promises no confidentiality on this branch.

tracks.legalName: Business Screening Service Dispute for Correction or Deletion of Criminal History Record Information (10 M.R.S. c. 239, § 1500-CC)
tracks.publicName: Getting a sealed record off a background check
tracks.mechanism: Chapter 239 regulates how a business screening service handles Maine criminal history record information. A business screening service under § 1500-AA is a person regularly engaged in the business of collecting, assembling, evaluating or disseminating criminal history record information about specific individuals for a fee, excluding a government entity and the news media. Under § 1500-CC, where the completeness or accuracy of a record is disputed by its subject, the service shall investigate WITHOUT CHARGE; must review and consider all relevant information the subject submits and determine whether its record accurately reflects the official record maintained by the State Bureau of Identification; must correct a record that does not accurately reflect the official record; and — the operative remedy here — if the disputed record is found to be sealed or the subject of a pardon, SHALL PROMPTLY DELETE the record. The service may terminate an investigation it reasonably determines is frivolous, but must then state the specific reasons and describe the information it needs. Within thirty days of receiving notice of the dispute the service must notify the subject of the results, including whether the investigation was completed or terminated and what records were corrected or deleted. Section 1500-DD requires a service disseminating records collected on or after 1 July 2010 to include the collection date and a notice that the information may include records that have been sealed or otherwise become inaccessible since. Section 1500-EE provides an FCRA safe harbour, deems foreign-corporation screening services to consent to Maine jurisdiction, and supplies a private right of action. Enacted by PL 2025, c. 513, § 1 and effective 29 July 2026.
exclusions: Records held by the State Bureau of Identification or any other criminal justice agency. Chapter 239 binds business screening services only; the agency record is corrected under 16 M.R.S. § 709.
Court records, which chapter 239 does not reach.
A government entity or the news media, both expressly excluded from the § 1500-AA definition of a business screening service.

The statutory remedy of $1,000 or actual damages, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees, under § 1500-EE(3). That is litigation and it is outside self-help. LegalEase does not plead it, demand it, threaten it, or calculate it.
A Fair Credit Reporting Act claim. § 1500-EE makes compliance with the relevant FCRA provisions a safe harbour and liability attaches only where conduct violates both, which is attorney analysis.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Seal Conviction for Victims of Sex Trafficking or Sexual Exploitation (15 M.R.S. § 2262-B)
tracks.publicName: Sealing a conviction connected to trafficking or exploitation
tracks.mechanism: Section 2262-B provides that criminal history record information relating to an eligible criminal conviction as described in § 2261(6)(C) must be sealed if the person filing the motion establishes, first, that the person has been a victim of sex trafficking or sexual exploitation, and second, that the commission of the crime for which the person was convicted was a substantial result of that sex trafficking or sexual exploitation. A motion under the section may be filed AT ANY TIME after the criminal conviction is entered. Section 2261(6)(C) defines an eligible criminal conviction for a § 2262-B motion as a criminal conviction for ANY current or former crime: there is no class limit, no chapter 11 exclusion and no offence list. Section 2261(8) defines sex trafficking and § 2261(9) defines sexual exploitation as engaging in the exchange of sex for money or resources because of a person's history of trauma, adverse childhood experiences, substance use disorder or other circumstances of victimization, exploitation or oppression. Section 2264(4-A) provides for remote participation by the person and any witnesses unless the court finds the person or a witness resides in Maine and the interests of justice require in-person participation; provides that official documentation of victim status is NOT required, and that if presented it creates a presumption that the person's participation in the offence was a substantial result of the trafficking or exploitation; and enumerates qualifying documentation, including an official record, certification or eligibility letter from a federal, state, tribal or local proceeding including a federal immigration approval notice, an affidavit or sworn testimony from clergy, a medical professional, victim services staff or another professional, and any other evidence the court finds of sufficient credibility or probative value. Section 2264(5) requires a hearing on a motion under the chapter EXCEPT that for a motion under § 2262-B the court may grant the motion without a hearing if the representative for the State consents. Section 2264(7), as amended, does not apply to records sealed under § 2262-A or § 2262-B, so a later conviction does not unseal and there is no self-reporting duty. Enacted by PL 2025, c. 513 and effective 29 July 2026.
exclusions: None on the face of the statute as to offence. § 2261(6)(C) reaches a conviction for any current or former crime, with no class limit, no Title 17-A chapter 11 exclusion and no offence list. This is by a wide margin the broadest sealing route in Maine.

No waiting period, no sentence-completion requirement, no pending-charge restriction and no case-count limit apply. The motion may be filed at any time after the conviction is entered, including while the person is still serving the sentence.

What the route does exclude is a case in which the two statutory elements cannot be established. That is a merits question for the participant and their advocate, not an eligibility filter LegalEase applies.

packetInstructions: Maine seals; it does not expunge. The Judicial Branch says in terms that Maine does not have expungement and the record is not completely erased. Never use 'expungement' in Maine participant copy.

Treat as no fee, confirm with the clerk, and do not promise a refund. Do not send the participant to CV-067 or CV-191: the $60 line applies to motions under the Maine Rules of Civil Procedure, and a sealing motion is filed in the underlying criminal proceeding.

Participant-facing copy must say that sealing restricts what criminal justice agencies may disseminate and what appears on a State Bureau of Identification background check, and must not say or imply that the court case disappears.

Official documentation is not required by § 2264(4-A)(B). If presented it creates a presumption that participation in the offence was a substantial result of the trafficking or exploitation. Frame the question so a no carries no implication, and never ask the participant to produce proof.

There is no waiting period, no sentence-completion requirement, no pending-charge restriction and no offence limit, and the motion may be filed while the person is still serving the sentence. This route is far broader than the prostitution route and participants on that route are screened into this one.
There is no self-reporting duty on this track and a later conviction does not unseal a § 2262-B record.
scopeRestrictions: Do not open this track without a named legal-aid or victim-services referral partner in place. This is the highest-value new relief in Maine and also the one where a bad automated experience does the most harm.

releaseBlockers.question: Form CR-308 page 2 carries a warning box stating that if at any time after the date of the order the defendant is convicted of a new crime in Maine or in any other jurisdiction, the new conviction extinguishes the order. That is inconsistent with 15 M.R.S. § 2264(7) as amended by PL 2025, c. 513, which now provides in terms that the subsection does not apply to records sealed pursuant to section 2262-A or 2262-B. Both the form and the amendment take effect 29 July 2026, so this is a live conflict on the face of two current official sources rather than a stale-form problem. LegalEase does not resolve it: the packet states the statutory rule, does not repeat the form's warning as advice, and carries the conflict as a release blocker.

releaseBlockers.question: Whether a chapter 310-A sealing order removes the case from Maine's public court record search. 15 M.R.S. § 2265 makes the conviction confidential criminal history record information and restricts dissemination by a criminal justice agency, and § 2264(6) makes the State Bureau of Identification amend its records. But 16 M.R.S. § 708(3)(A) provides that the Criminal History Record Information Act does not apply to criminal history record information contained in the records of public judicial proceedings retained by the District Court, Superior Court or Supreme Judicial Court, and that public access to those records is as provided by rule or administrative order of the Supreme Judicial Court. § 2265 opens 'Notwithstanding Title 16, section 704' and does not mention section 708. Participant-facing copy must therefore say that sealing restricts what criminal justice agencies may disseminate and what appears on a State Bureau of Identification check, and must not say or imply that the court case disappears from a public docket search.

unresolvedQuestions.question: Whether a chapter 310-A sealing order removes the case from Maine's public court record search. 15 M.R.S. § 2265 makes the conviction confidential criminal history record information and restricts dissemination by a criminal justice agency, and § 2264(6) makes the State Bureau of Identification amend its records. But 16 M.R.S. § 708(3)(A) provides that the Criminal History Record Information Act does not apply to criminal history record information contained in the records of public judicial proceedings retained by the District Court, Superior Court or Supreme Judicial Court, and that public access to those records is as provided by rule or administrative order of the Supreme Judicial Court. § 2265 opens 'Notwithstanding Title 16, section 704' and does not mention section 708. tracks.publicName: Application to set aside a conviction
tracks.mechanism: The ordinary application route. Not more than 3 felonies total, not more than 2 assaultive-crime convictions in a lifetime, and not more than 1 felony for the same offence where that offence is punishable by more than 10 years; misdemeanours are otherwise unlimited. Deferred-and-dismissed cases count as misdemeanour convictions against those determinations. Relief is discretionary under MCL 780.621d(13) and (14). MC 227 is the SCAO-approved statewide form and MCL 780.621d(7) prescribes seven categories of required content without which the application is invalid.
exclusions: A felony, or attempt, punishable by life imprisonment.
Violations or attempted violations of MCL 750.136b(3), 750.136d(1)(b) or (c), 750.145c, 750.145d, 750.520c, 750.520d and 750.520g.
MCL 750.520e where the conviction occurred on or after January 12, 2015.

Traffic offences: operating while intoxicated by any person; any traffic offence by a commercial-endorsement holder committed while operating a commercial motor vehicle or otherwise a commercial motor vehicle violation; any traffic offence causing injury or death.
A felony domestic violence conviction where the person has a previous misdemeanour domestic violence conviction.
Human trafficking offences under MCL 750.462a to 750.462h and terrorism offences under MCL 750.543a to 750.543z.
Out-of-state and federal convictions, which are outside the act.

packetInstructions: Michigan says set aside, not expunge. The statute, the SCAO forms and court filings all use set-aside; expungement appears only in Attorney General consumer materials and must not be used in generated documents.

State plainly what a set-aside does not reach: the Secretary of State driving record survives, SORA registration and reporting obligations continue for a listed offence, firearm rights are not restored, restitution obligations survive, and no fine, costs or other money paid is returned.

The court may not act on the application until Michigan State Police reports its record check to the court under MCL 780.621d(8). Tell the participant to expect that wait; it is a procedural gate on the court, not on generating the packet.

Make five copies of the application and all attachments and take them to the clerk, then mail to MSP, the Attorney General and the prosecuting official and complete the Proof of Service on both remaining copies.
Do not generate a proposed order. MC 228 is court-generated.

participantQuestions: Ask about every completed deferral. Under MCL 780.621(2) a deferred-and-dismissed disposition counts as a misdemeanour conviction for set-aside eligibility, and MCL 780.621d(7)(d) requires every such action to be listed on the application. Omitting it makes the application facially deficient.
Do not automate One Bad Night grouping. Ask whether convictions arose from the same incident within 24 hours and route to counsel where an exception may break the grouping.
scopeRestrictions: A separate application is required for each convicting court. Convictions may be combined on one application only where all of them are in the same court, and clerks are directed to watch for applications that improperly combine convictions from different courts.

tracks.legalName: Application to Set Aside Misdemeanor Marihuana Conviction(s) under MCL 780.621e
tracks.publicName: Set aside a misdemeanor marijuana conviction
tracks.mechanism: Added by 2020 PA 192, effective April 11, 2021. Reaches a misdemeanour marihuana offence as defined at MCL 780.621e(7): a violation of MCL 333.7403(2)(d), MCL 333.7404(2)(d), or a marihuana paraphernalia violation of MCL 333.7453, or a substantially corresponding local ordinance. Filing raises a rebuttable presumption that the conviction was based on activity that would not have been a crime if committed on or after December 6, 2018, and the evidentiary burden rests solely on the objecting prosecuting agency. Absent a timely answer the court must enter the order.
exclusions: Anything broader than the MCL 780.621e(7) definition. Nothing outside MCL 333.7403(2)(d), MCL 333.7404(2)(d), MCL 333.7453 or a substantially corresponding local ordinance.

tracks.legalName: Application to Set Aside a First-Violation Operating While Intoxicated Conviction
tracks.publicName: Set aside a first drunk-driving conviction
tracks.mechanism: 2021 PA 78, effective February 19, 2022, carved a first-violation operating-while-intoxicated offence back in against an otherwise categorical traffic exclusion. The offence is a violation of MCL 257.625(1), (2), (3), (6) or (8), or a corresponding tribal, other-state, federal or local provision, committed by an individual who at the time of the violation had no prior MCL 257.625 convictions. Once only, and excluded from automatic relief by MCL 780.621g(10).
exclusions: An operating-while-intoxicated conviction where the person had any prior MCL 257.625 conviction at the time of the violation.
A second application after a first-violation OWI conviction has already been set aside.
Automatic relief, which excludes OWI committed by any person under MCL 780.621g(10).

tracks.legalName: Application by a Human Trafficking Victim to Set Aside Conviction(s)
tracks.publicName: Set aside a conviction you got because you were trafficked
tracks.mechanism: Convictions under MCL 750.448, 750.449 or 750.450, or a substantially corresponding local ordinance, where the person committed the offence as a direct result of being a victim of a human trafficking violation. No waiting period; it may be filed at any time following conviction and more than one conviction may be set aside. The applicant must prove by a preponderance that the conviction was a direct result of being a victim, and the MCL 780.621d(13) public-welfare finding still applies. MCL 780.621d(7)(g) requires a statement of the facts supporting the trafficking contention.
exclusions: Convictions outside MCL 750.448, 750.449 and 750.450 or a substantially corresponding local ordinance.

tracks.legalName: Set-Aside of a Pre-2015 Fourth-Degree Criminal Sexual Conduct Conviction
tracks.publicName: Clearing a fourth-degree criminal sexual conduct conviction from before 2015
tracks.mechanism: A violation or attempted violation of MCL 750.520e committed before January 12, 2015 may be set aside, subject to a bespoke prior-record test: the individual must not have been convicted of another offence other than not more than two minor offences, where a minor offence is a misdemeanour or ordinance violation with a maximum term not exceeding 90 days and a maximum fine of not more than $1,000, committed by a person not more than 21 years old. Convictions on or after January 12, 2015 are categorically excluded by MCL 780.621c(c).
exclusions: Convictions on or after January 12, 2015, which MCL 780.621c(c) categorically excludes.
An individual convicted of any other offence beyond not more than two minor offences as defined.

tracks.publicName: Felony convictions that clear on their own
tracks.mechanism: Effective April 11, 2023, up to two felony convictions are set aside by operation of law without any application, ten years after either imposition of sentence or completion of any term of imprisonment with the Michigan Department of Corrections, whichever occurs later. No court order is required; SCAO guidance states all eligible convictions are set aside by operation of law.
exclusions: Assaultive crimes, serious misdemeanours and crimes of dishonesty.
Any other offence punishable by 10 or more years.
Any offence listed in MCL 777.1 to 777.69 whose elements involve a minor, a vulnerable adult, injury or serious impairment, or death.
Any violation related to human trafficking.
The three traffic categories, including operating while intoxicated committed by any person under MCL 780.621g(10).
Criminal charges pending in the Michigan State Police criminal history record database, or a conviction of any criminal offence recorded in that database during the applicable period.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Set-Aside of Misdemeanours Punishable by 92 Days or Less under MCL 780.621g(1) and (3)
tracks.publicName: Lower-level misdemeanours that clear on their own
tracks.mechanism: Set aside seven years after imposition of sentence with no numerical limit. Two different actors depending on where the record lives: where the conviction is recorded and maintained in the Michigan State Police criminal history database, meaning fingerprints were submitted, MSP sets it aside under subsection (3); where the conviction is maintained only in the court's case management system, the court must set it aside under subsection (1), and each court must notify the arresting law enforcement agency on or before the tenth day of each month for the preceding month.
exclusions: Assaultive crimes, serious misdemeanours and crimes of dishonesty.
Any other offence punishable by 10 or more years.
Any offence listed in MCL 777.1 to 777.69 whose elements involve a minor, a vulnerable adult, injury or serious impairment, or death.
Any violation related to human trafficking.
The three traffic categories, including operating while intoxicated committed by any person under MCL 780.621g(10).
Criminal charges pending in the Michigan State Police criminal history record database, or a conviction of any criminal offence recorded in that database during the applicable period.

waitingPeriods.duration: 7 years, automatic, with no numerical limit

tracks.legalName: Destruction of Biometric Data and Arrest Card After Acquittal or Dismissal under MCL 28.243
tracks.publicName: Clearing fingerprints and an arrest card after a case ended in your favour
tracks.mechanism: SCAO form MC 262, Order of Acquittal/Dismissal or Remand, carries the notice that the defendant's fingerprints and arrest card will be destroyed by Michigan State Police within 60 days of the order when permitted by MCL 28.243, and the clerk must advise the MSP Criminal Justice Information Center of the disposition under MCL 769.16a. Under MCL 28.243(8)(b), where the prosecutor agrees at any time after dismissal, or where neither the prosecutor nor the judge objects within 60 days of the dismissal order, the arrest record, all biometric data and fingerprints are destroyed and any LEIN entry is removed. MSP acts on receipt of an appropriate district or circuit court order.
exclusions: MCL 28.243(14): a person arraigned for enumerated offences, including the commission or attempted commission of a crime with or against a child under 16, and, materially for this population, a person who has a prior conviction other than a misdemeanour traffic offence.

waitingPeriods.condition: Entry of the order of acquittal or dismissal
waitingPeriods.duration: 60 days for MSP destruction; for a dismissal, where neither the prosecutor nor the judge objects within 60 days

tracks.legalName: Completed Deferrals and Their Record Consequences
tracks.publicName: What a completed deferral means for clearing your record
tracks.mechanism: Three things are simultaneously true for a participant with a completed deferral. The case record is already nonpublic by operation of the deferral statute, so there is usually nothing to set aside on the court side. The arrest record may still exist and is addressed by the biometric-destruction routes rather than the set-aside act. And under MCL 780.621(2) the deferred-and-dismissed disposition counts as a misdemeanour conviction for determining set-aside eligibility, with MCL 780.621d(7)(d) requiring every such action to be listed on any application.
exclusions: This is not relief. It alters no record and must not be counted as a paid packet mechanism or a substantive relief mechanism.
